files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

edits.description: publish: small changes Claude makes to the file at `file_path` in this same call, instead of editing the file with Edit and publishing after. Use it on a page (add `url` to update an artifact from another conversation) or on one data file of an artifact made from a type (its `url`, with that file as `file_path`). Not allowed with `type_url` or `files`. Each old_str is text copied exactly from the file as it now stands and must occur in it exactly once; new_str takes its place (empty deletes it). The edits apply in order, all or none: the file is published with them and then saved with them on disk, so it stays the source for later changes; on a miss nothing is changed or published, and the result says which edit failed and why.

old_str.description: Text copied exactly from the file; must occur once.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes the published path of a `files` entry. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` is served at its path relative to `root`, unless a `files` map entry states its served path. Claude sends it with every such publish, set to the folder that holds the Artifact's files at their served paths.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

page_token.description: list only: the `next_page_token` a listing of the same scope gave, to list the artifacts after it.

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (writing people will keep editing or pass around as text, such as a memo, plan, spec, proposal or notes), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (a page to look at or use: an explainer, a diagram, anything interactive, a dashboard that shows data, anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}). content.content:
# Rawls run: who or what is an affected entity?

**Status:** a manual run of the Rawls step (the module is designed, not built;
README, "Rawls"). Every judgement here is a proposal: witness
`llm:claude-opus-5-5 prompt=unrecorded`, interactive session 2026-11-05.
It generates questions; it does not answer them. **The veil generates the
question; standing answers it.**

**Asked by Sloane, 2026-11-05**, for open question Q29 (governments and
places): "what's the most appropriate and resilient way to define this when
many of the relevant blocks are going to be changing", making "space for
other consciousnesses in this schema" (her estimate: roughly a 10–12% chance
that whales can talk to us in some way within 20 years), and working at "what
is the affected entity ... in the most Cartesian way we can." She also noted
that location can mean an IP address, "a particularly high value indicator,
especially if you're joined to a private network."

## 1. Behind the veil: positions we might occupy

If we did not know which of these we would be, what would we want the schema
to do?

| Position | What a careless schema does to it |
|---|---|
| A stateless person, or a refugee | Requires a government link it cannot supply; treats it as missing data |
| A trans person whose documents don't match | Makes the document-issuer's record the person's identity |
| A person in a place where dissent is dangerous | Stores an IP address that locates and endangers them |
| A person on a private or institutional network | Leaks membership of that network through the address |
| A person with no fixed address | Fails a location check it can never pass |
| A member of an Indigenous nation | Records only the state's claim over its land and people |
| A child, or a person speaking through a guardian | Has no way to be represented by someone else |
| Someone in a disputed place | Gets one government chosen for them as the default |
| A household, co-operative or community | Must be flattened into individuals or into an organisation |
| A person not yet born | Has interests, no voice and no record |
| A dead person, or their estate | Disappears, though their data and rights persist |
| An individual animal; a whale pod; a species | Appears only as a resource (the SDG crosswalk found exactly this) |
| A river or ecosystem with legal personhood in some jurisdictions | Cannot be an entity at all |
| An AI system, or a human acting with an agent | Is either a person or nothing |

**The hard version.** If this list feels complete, we stopped too soon. In
fifty years, which entities will seem obviously missing? We can't see that
from here. The schema has to be able to add them without being rebuilt.

## 2. The Cartesian minimum

Start from what can be checked, and add nothing that can't.

1. **An entity is an opaque id of ours.** Nothing about it (kind, name,
   location, government) is part of the key. Kind is itself a claim.
2. **Everything else is a dated claim with a witness.** "This entity is a
   human", "is a whale", "lives in this place", "holds documents from this
   government", "speaks for that entity": each is a claim, made by someone, at
   a time, on evidence, checkable or not. Frameworks' assertions (ISO, the UN,
   a government) are claims like any other, attributed to their maker.
3. **Three separate layers, never merged:**
   - **Standing:** that the entity exists and can be affected, and who
     attests to it.
   - **Interests:** what can harm or benefit it. Evidence of sentience or
     welfare goes here, with its witness. Interests don't need a voice.
   - **Voice:** whether it can speak for itself, and if not, who speaks for
     it (guardian, proxy, community, representative), recorded as a relation
     the represented entity, or its recognised advocates, can contest.
4. **The identity ring is a verification level on claims, not a type.** "A
   human with a name and a location" is a ring of verified claims. A whale
   pod could have its own ring (identified, located, represented) without
   being forced into the human one.
5. **Open vocabularies.** Kinds, documents and relations are values in a
   versioned list, never a closed enum. Adding "cetacean" or "river" is a
   data change.

## 3. Resilience: the blocks that will change

Governments form and dissolve, documents change format, networks are
re-addressed, and our understanding of who can speak will move. So:

- **No external block is ever a key.** ISO codes, passport numbers, IP
  addresses and government ids are dated relations, never identifiers.
- **Every relation carries `as_of` and a witness**, so a change appends
  rather than overwrites, and the history survives.
- **Claims can be contested and forked** (the dissent model): an entity, or
  its advocates, can dispute how it is described, without one version being
  presented as the default.

## 3a. In practice, most people sign in with someone else's identity

Sloane, 2026-11-05: "most people are going to use OAuth anyway, and they're
just going to use their Apple ID." So for most people the first issuer is not
a government but a platform (Apple, Google, Microsoft, through WorkOS). The
same rule applies: the sign-in provider is a dated relation with a witness,
never the key. An account can link several providers, lose one, or move.
What each provider asserts (a verified email, a relay address like Apple's
Hide My Email, sometimes a name) is that provider's claim. Questions: does a
provider's assertion count toward "a human with a name", or only toward "a
controller of this account"? What happens to someone whose platform account
is closed? Does relying on two or three platforms concentrate the very power
the identity ring is meant to keep out?

## 4. Location, and the IP address

Location is the most dangerous field in the ring.

| Kind | Precision | Sensitivity | Proposed default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Declared place | coarse, chosen by the entity | low | the only location the identity ring needs |
| Observed network location (IP) | can be precise; on a private network it reveals membership | high | never stored raw; never published; used only transiently for security, then discarded or kept as a salted digest with a short expiry |
| Physical coordinates | precise | highest | only when the entity chooses, for a stated use |

Questions: does "a specific location" in the identity ring mean declared
place only? Who may ever see an observed one? What do we hold if a
government demands it?

## 5. Questions this run cannot answer (for people with standing)

1. What should the ring ask of a stateless person, and who should design
   that? (Refugee and statelessness organisations; stateless people.)
2. How should a trans person's record handle documents that contradict them,
   beyond making the document link optional? (Trans people; trans legal
   advocates.)
3. Who may speak for a whale, a pod or a river, and how is a guardian's
   claim contested? (Animal-cognition researchers, rights-of-nature lawyers,
   Indigenous nations whose law already recognises such standing.)
4. What evidence should "interests" require for a non-human, and should the
   threshold differ by kind? (Sentience researchers; welfare law.)
5. How do Indigenous nations appear: as governments, as peoples, or as
   something this schema hasn't named? (Indigenous data-sovereignty bodies;
   CARE principles.)
6. When an entity can newly speak (a whale, a future AI), how does its own
   account of itself enter and outrank what others said about it?
7. What location data would we refuse to hold even if asked, and is that
   refusal written down before anyone asks? (Digital-rights organisations.)
8. Who is missing from section 1? Ask the people in it.

## Related

- Praxis Q30 (identity) and Q29 (governments and places).
- The verification half: Dark `docs/praxis/identity-verification-topology.md`
  (branch `claude/identity-ring`): no-documents baseline, pairwise keys,
  standing ladder S0-S3, assertion families, assurance levels L0-L4.

## What this run does not do

It does not choose the word for governments, decide the schema, or settle any
question above. It is input to Q29 and to the Rawls module's design: a worked
example of an evaluation made behind the veil, with its witness recorded.

| Declared place | coarse, chosen by the entity | low | the only location the identity ring needs |
| Observed network location (IP) | can be precise; on a private network it reveals membership | high | never stored raw; never published; used only transiently for security, then discarded or kept as a salted digest with a short expiry |
| Physical coordinates | precise | highest | only when the entity chooses, for a stated use |

Questions: does "a specific location" in the identity ring mean declared
place only? Who may ever see an observed one? What do we hold if a
government demands it?

## 5. Questions this run cannot answer (for people with standing)

1. What should the ring ask of a stateless person, and who should design
   that? (Refugee and statelessness organisations; stateless people.)
2. How should a trans person's record handle documents that contradict them,
   beyond making the document link optional? (Trans people; trans legal
   advocates.)
3. Who may speak for a whale, a pod or a river, and how is a guardian's
   claim contested? (Animal-cognition researchers, rights-of-nature lawyers,
   Indigenous nations whose law already recognises such standing.)
4. What evidence should "interests" require for a non-human, and should the
   threshold differ by kind? (Sentience researchers; welfare law.)
5. How do Indigenous nations appear: as governments, as peoples, or as
   something this schema hasn't named? (Indigenous data-sovereignty bodies;
   CARE principles.)
6. When an entity can newly speak (a whale, a future AI), how does its own
   account of itself enter and outrank what others said about it?
7. What location data would we refuse to hold even if asked, and is that
   refusal written down before anyone asks? (Digital-rights organisations.)
8. Who is missing from section 1? Ask the people in it.

## Related

- Praxis Q30 (identity) and Q29 (governments and places).
- The verification half: Dark `docs/praxis/identity-verification-topology.md`
  (branch `claude/identity-ring`): no-documents baseline, pairwise keys,
  standing ladder S0-S3, assertion families, assurance levels L0-L4.

## What this run does not do

It does not choose the word for governments, decide the schema, or settle any
question above. It is input to Q29 and to the Rawls module's design: a worked
example of an evaluation made behind the veil, with its witness recorded.

# Praxis identity verification topology — draft 1

2026-11-05. For Sloane's review. Builds on the master plan's community-evidence rules
(`docs/coordination/praxis-master-plan.md` ~809-835): participation, identity
assurance and public attribution are separate; continuity is not identity;
organization representation needs its own evidence; "identity checked" names the
actual check. Companion: `~/tray/praxis-action-attestation-profile.md`.
Web facts were checked 2026-11-05; sources inline. UNVERIFIED means not confirmed.

## 0. Baseline: assume no documents at all

Design case: a stateless person (e.g. a Palestinian refugee) with no state ID we can
| D Document | A government issuer vouches for attributes | mDL / digital ID, ID document + selfie vendor, passport digital ID |
| X Context | History only the real person shares with us | Existing correspondence, meeting record, custodian account details matching |
| H Human | A trusted person confirms | Video call, in-person, call-back via official switchboard, vouching by a verified client, notary |
| R Representation | Speaks for an organization | Official website challenge, staff/press-office confirmation, org domain |

## 2. Assurance levels (proposed)

| Level | Requirement | Use |
|---|---|---|
| L0 Continuity | P | Pseudonymous participation; same commenter returning |
| L1 Reachable | P + C | Public comments under a display name |
| L2 Known | P + C + X | Existing clients today (email + conversation history) |
| L3 Verified | P + C + D, or P + C + X + H | Client onboarding; claimed-real-name public attribution |
| L4 High-stakes | L3 + fresh H, from a different family than the one being changed | Bank/address change, withdrawal instructions, agreement changes |
| Rep (separate axis) | R + H through an independent official channel | "Office of …" attribution |

## 3. Method catalog

| Method | Family | Strength | Weakness / surveillance cost | Free-software path | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Passkey | P | Phishing-resistant continuity | Not identity; synced passkeys inherit the cloud account (NIST SP 800-63B-4 synced appendix) | Self-hosted Supabase Auth | Planned |
| Email / existing correspondence | C + X | Works now; rich context for existing clients | Mailbox compromise; staff-held mailboxes | Inbox already holds it | **Usable now** |
| mDL via Digital Credentials API | D | Issuer-signed, selective disclosure, no issuer "phone home" (Apple) | Coverage gaps; Apple gates website requests through Business Connect registration and app use through a revocable entitlement | Multipaz verifier (OpenWallet Foundation) | Safari 26 and Chrome 141 ship the API |
| — Utah specifically | D | Utah SB 275 (2026) bans issuer tracking, requires selective disclosure, wallet choice, and a **verifier duty of loyalty and minimization** — binds us | Utah is **not** in Apple Wallet's verify list; current Utah mDL (GET Mobile ID app) sunsets 2027-01-01 | — | Wait for the new state program |
| Doc + selfie vendor | D | Covers anyone with a physical ID | Centralized biometrics. Stripe keeps 1 yr by default; ID.me keeps a face gallery; Persona can redact immediately (templates ≤3 yr otherwise). BIPA exposure falls on us too | None | Fallback only; Persona with immediate redaction is the least invasive found |
| Custodian identity check reuse | D/X | Already done by the custodian | Whether an RIA may formally rely on it is UNVERIFIED | — | Use as a context match, not a formal reliance |
| Remote online notarization | H + D | Statutory in Utah; strong | Each session video-recorded and journaled; cost | — | For L4 edge cases |
| Video call / in-person | H | Strong against impersonation | Effort; deepfake risk on video | — | Usable now |
| Vouching by a verified client | H | Fits the community model | Collusion; social pressure | Signed vouch record | Proposed |
| Official-domain email challenge | C/R | Proves control of an office mailbox | A staffer may hold it; Senate address patterns UNVERIFIED | — | Usable |
| Website / DNS / Bluesky domain proof | C/R | Cryptographically checkable; proves the office controls the domain | Proves office, not person | Keyoxide, Bluesky handle resolution | Usable |
| Switchboard / press-office call-back | H/R | Journalism standard | Slow | — | Usable |

## 4. Worked cases

- **Existing client, today:** L2 from email + correspondence. Add a passkey on first Praxis login.
- **New client onboarding:** L3. Order: mDL if their state is supported → otherwise human check (video call) + context → vendor with immediate redaction only if they choose it. Record the method used and keep no image unless the law requires it.

# Praxis identity and tenancy model

**Status:** proposed. CIO decisions recorded 2026-10-10 (later answers: each of the 24 active clients with no linked account gets an org; k-unit gets a new relationship type); CIO answers 2026-10-12 (ETH-t4h4x.15: orgs and households are the SAME entity — generalize to `orgs` with `org_type` firm/household/individual; `crm.households` superseded, seed household orgs from Altruist not from that table); schema below is not yet built.
**Ticket:** ETH-t4h4x.15 (parent ETH-t4h4x). Related: ETH-t4h4x.12 (grants dashboard), ETH-t4h4x.14 (Postgres isolation spike), ETH-afrdc (org-less admission), ETH-mbztw (WorkOS sync), ETH-fiaua (empty `household_members`).

One definition of who a person is, which org they belong to, and what that org may see. It replaces six partial models.

## CIO decisions (2026-10-10)

1. **The tenant is an org row.** It is 1:1 with a WorkOS org, and people are its members. The CIO reviews firms one by one.
2. **Relationship type lives in the DB, as data rather than an enum.** Eventually orgs define their own types (for example, paid enterprise Praxis orgs). That part comes later.
3. **Person funnel:** anonymous → contact → free user (onboarding) → one of:
   - Praxis (paying) user
   - free user forever
   - asset-management client
4. **Asset-management client status comes from Altruist,** not from a hand-set field. It automatically includes Praxis access.
5. **Households use a membership table with roles.** Shared emails are allowed, because some client pairs share one inbox.
6. **Per-org data grants cover all org data,** not just tick scores, and are editable from a dashboard (ETH-t4h4x.12). Defaults:
   - `current_tick` is Ethical Capital-only.
   - `strategy` and `weight` are visible to clients, including paying Praxis users.
7. **Lavender is the highest Praxis tier:** full access to the resources we host (prime enterprise). It is a Praxis tier, not a relationship type. k-unit (Kevin) is Lavender.
8. **Household seed:** start from Altruist's 53 household names. Prospects get household orgs too.
9. **Junk rows:** `clients.clients` ids 2 (Acme Corp), 96 and 97 are junk (ETH-mz0wv).

## CIO direction (2026-11-05): the identity ring

10. **The base identity ring proves only that you are a human being with a
    specific name and location.** Associating yourself with a country, or
    any other place-level framework, is optional: the person chooses it, and
    it is never required or inferred from their documents. In the CIO's
    words: "the identity ring should be prove that you're a human being with
    a specific name and location. Then, if you want to associate yourself
    with a country, you can do it, but it's an option." The reason she gave:
    "is it really the case that your identity should be tied to the people
    who issue your documents?" The same principle governs the Praxis places
    layer: a framework's treatment of a place is that framework's assertion,
    recorded as a relation (Praxis `resources/topologies/countries/`).
    Open: what counts as proof of a name and a location, and how the ring
    keeps location private.

Design case: a stateless person (e.g. a Palestinian refugee) with no state ID we can
check, and good reasons not to hand over what they do have. Documents are an
optional upgrade on top of this baseline, never the floor.

**Three different questions:**

| Question | Answer without documents |
|---|---|
| Is this identifier unique? | Yes, trivially: the person generates a key pair on their own device; the identifier is derived from the public key. We issue nothing and hold no secret. |
| Is this one person, not one of many accounts they control? | Not provable from the key. Handled by not letting standing scale with account count (below), plus bounded vouching. |
| What standing do they have? | Earned from conduct, relationships and the kind of claim, not from papers. |

**Identifier rules (proposed):**
- Self-generated key; Praxis stores the public half only.
- Pairwise by default: a different identifier per context, so a refugee's comment
  identity can't be linked to anything else unless they choose to link it.
- Recovery without documents: the person names guardians (other people, or their
  own second device) who can jointly rotate the key; rotation is announced to them.
- No nationality, legal name, photo or biometric collected at this level.

**Standing ladder (proposed):**

| Standing | Earned by | Grants |
|---|---|---|
| S0 Present | Holding a key | Read, ask questions, submit evidence and comments for review |
| S1 Continuous | Consistent use over time; record of conduct | Public attribution under a chosen name; replies; reputation on their own record |
| S2 Vouched | Vouches from people or organizations with standing (bounded: each voucher has a limited number; vouches are signed and revocable) | Weight in community review; invite others |
| S3 Corroborated | Basis of knowledge for a specific claim checked (evidence origin, consistency, independent corroboration) | That claim admitted as evidence, attributed as they choose |

Standing attaches to **the claim and the record**, not to legal identity. A first-hand
account is judged on provenance and corroboration (plan rule: bind source
authentication, evidence origin and basis of knowledge). Community opinion already
confers no control in Praxis, so a person running many accounts gains little.

**Where documents become unavoidable:** a custodied investment account. The
custodian's identity rules require a document (a passport or other government ID
for non-US persons); whether they accept refugee travel documents or UN-issued
papers varies by custodian (UNVERIFIED). Praxis can be honest about that boundary
without making it a condition of participating.

**Harms to design against:** collecting data that endangers the person if it leaks or
is compelled; requiring an organization's registration (UN or NGO) as a gate, since
it can itself be a target (HRW reported in 2021 that UNHCR-collected Rohingya data
was shared with Myanmar via Bangladesh); biometrics at any level below client custody.

A trail captures project intent across repositories and branches. Manage intent and discussions on the whole trail; use --repo and --branch to select context for checkout, sessions, findings, and approvals.

Usage:
  entire trail [flags]
  entire trail [command]

Available Commands:
  approvals       List approval decisions on a trail
  approve         Approve a trail
  checkout        Check out a trail's branch
  comment         Discuss the whole trail across repositories
  create          Create a trail and publish its branch
  finding         Manage a trail's agent findings
  link            Link a repository branch to a trail
  list            List trails in a project
  merge           Merge one of a trail's changes into its base
  resume          Resume a trail's agent session
  show            Show trail intent and its repositories and branches
  unlink          Unlink a repository branch without deleting its work
  update          Update project intent and lifecycle
  watch           Tail events for a trail's selected repository branch

Flags:
  -h, --help             help for trail
      --project string   Project as gh/<owner> or et/<project>; required for list, otherwise defaults to the repository's namespace
      --repo string      Target repository as forge/owner/repo (e.g. gh/acme/app) or a clone URL; for list, only filters the required --project

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

# Rawls run: who or what is an affected entity?

**Status:** a manual run of the Rawls step (the module is designed, not built;
README, "Rawls"). Every judgement here is a proposal: witness
`llm:claude-opus-5-5 prompt=unrecorded`, interactive session 2026-11-05.
It generates questions; it does not answer them. **The veil generates the
question; standing answers it.**

**Asked by Sloane, 2026-11-05**, for open question Q29 (governments and
places): "what's the most appropriate and resilient way to define this when
many of the relevant blocks are going to be changing", making "space for
other consciousnesses in this schema" (her estimate: roughly a 10–12% chance
that whales can talk to us in some way within 20 years), and working at "what
is the affected entity ... in the most Cartesian way we can." She also noted
that location can mean an IP address, "a particularly high value indicator,
especially if you're joined to a private network."

## 1. Behind the veil: positions we might occupy

If we did not know which of these we would be, what would we want the schema
to do?

| Position | What a careless schema does to it |
|---|---|
| A stateless person, or a refugee | Requires a government link it cannot supply; treats it as missing data |
| A trans person whose documents don't match | Makes the document-issuer's record the person's identity |
| A person in a place where dissent is dangerous | Stores an IP address that locates and endangers them |
| A person on a private or institutional network | Leaks membership of that network through the address |
| A person with no fixed address | Fails a location check it can never pass |
| A member of an Indigenous nation | Records only the state's claim over its land and people |
| A child, or a person speaking through a guardian | Has no way to be represented by someone else |
| Someone in a disputed place | Gets one government chosen for them as the default |
| A household, co-operative or community | Must be flattened into individuals or into an organisation |
| A person not yet born | Has interests, no voice and no record |
| A dead person, or their estate | Disappears, though their data and rights persist |
| An individual animal; a whale pod; a species | Appears only as a resource (the SDG crosswalk found exactly this) |
| A river or ecosystem with legal personhood in some jurisdictions | Cannot be an entity at all |
| An AI system, or a human acting with an agent | Is either a person or nothing |

**The hard version.** If this list feels complete, we stopped too soon. In
fifty years, which entities will seem obviously missing? We can't see that
from here. The schema has to be able to add them without being rebuilt.

## 2. The Cartesian minimum

Start from what can be checked, and add nothing that can't.

1. **An entity is an opaque id of ours.** Nothing about it (kind, name,
   location, government) is part of the key. Kind is itself a claim.
2. **Everything else is a dated claim with a witness.** "This entity is a
   human", "is a whale", "lives in this place", "holds documents from this
   government", "speaks for that entity": each is a claim, made by someone, at
   a time, on evidence, checkable or not. Frameworks' assertions (ISO, the UN,
   a government) are claims like any other, attributed to their maker.
3. **Three separate layers, never merged:**
   - **Standing:** that the entity exists and can be affected, and who
     attests to it.
   - **Interests:** what can harm or benefit it. Evidence of sentience or
     welfare goes here, with its witness. Interests don't need a voice.
   - **Voice:** whether it can speak for itself, and if not, who speaks for
     it (guardian, proxy, community, representative), recorded as a relation
     the represented entity, or its recognised advocates, can contest.
4. **The identity ring is a verification level on claims, not a type.** "A
   human with a name and a location" is a ring of verified claims. A whale
   pod could have its own ring (identified, located, represented) without
   being forced into the human one.
5. **Open vocabularies.** Kinds, documents and relations are values in a
   versioned list, never a closed enum. Adding "cetacean" or "river" is a
   data change.

## 3. Resilience: the blocks that will change

Governments form and dissolve, documents change format, networks are
re-addressed, and our understanding of who can speak will move. So:

- **No external block is ever a key.** ISO codes, passport numbers, IP
  addresses and government ids are dated relations, never identifiers.
- **Every relation carries `as_of` and a witness**, so a change appends
  rather than overwrites, and the history survives.
- **Claims can be contested and forked** (the dissent model): an entity, or
  its advocates, can dispute how it is described, without one version being
  presented as the default.

## 3a. In practice, most people sign in with someone else's identity

Sloane, 2026-11-05: "most people are going to use OAuth anyway, and they're
just going to use their Apple ID." So for most people the first issuer is not
a government but a platform (Apple, Google, Microsoft, through WorkOS). The
same rule applies: the sign-in provider is a dated relation with a witness,
never the key. An account can link several providers, lose one, or move.
What each provider asserts (a verified email, a relay address like Apple's
Hide My Email, sometimes a name) is that provider's claim. Questions: does a
provider's assertion count toward "a human with a name", or only toward "a
controller of this account"? What happens to someone whose platform account
is closed? Does relying on two or three platforms concentrate the very power
the identity ring is meant to keep out?

## 4. Location, and the IP address

Location is the most dangerous field in the ring.

| Kind | Precision | Sensitivity | Proposed default |
|---|---|---|---|
| Declared place | coarse, chosen by the entity | low | the only location the identity ring needs |
| Observed network location (IP) | can be precise; on a private network it reveals membership | high | never stored raw; never published; used only transiently for security, then discarded or kept as a salted digest with a short expiry |
| Physical coordinates | precise | highest | only when the entity chooses, for a stated use |

Questions: does "a specific location" in the identity ring mean declared
place only? Who may ever see an observed one? What do we hold if a
government demands it?

## 5. Questions this run cannot answer (for people with standing)

1. What should the ring ask of a stateless person, and who should design
   that? (Refugee and statelessness organisations; stateless people.)
2. How should a trans person's record handle documents that contradict them,
   beyond making the document link optional? (Trans people; trans legal
   advocates.)
3. Who may speak for a whale, a pod or a river, and how is a guardian's
   claim contested? (Animal-cognition researchers, rights-of-nature lawyers,
   Indigenous nations whose law already recognises such standing.)
4. What evidence should "interests" require for a non-human, and should the
   threshold differ by kind? (Sentience researchers; welfare law.)
5. How do Indigenous nations appear: as governments, as peoples, or as
   something this schema hasn't named? (Indigenous data-sovereignty bodies;
   CARE principles.)
6. When an entity can newly speak (a whale, a future AI), how does its own
   account of itself enter and outrank what others said about it?
7. What location data would we refuse to hold even if asked, and is that
   refusal written down before anyone asks? (Digital-rights organisations.)
8. Who is missing from section 1? Ask the people in it.

## Related

- Praxis Q30 (identity) and Q29 (governments and places).
- The verification half: Dark `docs/praxis/identity-verification-topology.md`
  (branch `claude/identity-ring`): no-documents baseline, pairwise keys,
  standing ladder S0-S3, assertion families, assurance levels L0-L4.

## What this run does not do

It does not choose the word for governments, decide the schema, or settle any
question above. It is input to Q29 and to the Rawls module's design: a worked
example of an evaluation made behind the veil, with its witness recorded.

def git(root, *args):
    return subprocess.run(['git', '-C', str(root), *args], env=GIT_ENV, check=True,
                          capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()


def write(root, rel, text):
    p = Path(root) / rel
    p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    p.write_text(text, encoding='utf-8')


QUESTIONS = """# Open questions

### Q1 · First
- **Context:** see `docs/a.md`.
- **Related:** Q2 decides the rest.

### Q2 · Second
- **Context:** nothing back.

### Q3 · Third
- **Related:** Q1, which links here: Q3? No, Q1 does not.
"""


class Fixture:
    """Two throwaway repositories: `home` (with OPENQUESTIONS.md) and `other`
    (with a document on branch `feature/x` only)."""

    def __init__(self, tmp):
        self.base = Path(tmp)
        self.home = self.base / 'home'
        self.other = self.base / 'other'
        for r in (self.home, self.other):
            r.mkdir()
            git(r, 'init', '-q', '-b', 'main')
        write(self.other, 'README.md', 'other\n')
        git(self.other, 'add', '.')
        git(self.other, 'commit', '-qm', 'init')
        git(self.other, 'checkout', '-qb', 'feature/x')
        write(self.other, 'docs/topo.md',
              '# Topology\n\n## Related\n\n- Home `docs/a.md` and open question Q1.\n'
              '- Home `docs/lonely.md`.\n\n'
              'It collects no location at all.\n')
        git(self.other, 'add', '.')
        git(self.other, 'commit', '-qm', 'topo')
        self.other_commit = git(self.other, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD')
        git(self.other, 'checkout', '-q', 'main')

        write(self.home, 'OPENQUESTIONS.md', QUESTIONS)
        write(self.home, 'docs/lonely.md', '# Lonely\n\nNo links at all.\n')
        write(self.home, 'docs/a.md',
              '# A\n\nSee `docs/b.md` and Q1. Commit HOMECOMMIT.\n\n## Related\n\n'
              '- `docs/b.md`\n- `docs/lonely.md`\n'
              '- Other `docs/topo.md` (branch `feature/x`)\n')
        write(self.home, 'docs/b.md', '# B\n\nBack to `docs/a.md`.\n')
        git(self.home, 'add', '.')
        git(self.home, 'commit', '-qm', 'init')
        self.home_commit = git(self.home, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD')

        self.assertIn('qid', {r.kind for r in refs})

              'Other `docs/topo.md` (branch `no/such`), Other `docs/topo.md`.\n')

        self.assertIn('UNRESOLVED\thome:docs/bad.md:3\tqid\tQ99', text)
        self.assertIn('UNRESOLVED\thome:docs/bad.md:3\tcommit\tabc1234', text)

        self.assertIn('not found at other@HEAD', text)

              '`other:README.md`, `the-other:README.md`, `other/README.md`, `nope:README.md`.\n')

        self.assertEqual([(r.repo, r.path, r.status) for r in refs],
                         [('other', 'README.md', 'ok')] * 3)

        write(self.f.home, 'docs/d.md', 'SHA-256 `a.tsv` 960c8c4b…fb97, and a `.tsv` file.\n')
        kinds = [(r.kind, r.raw) for r in self.f.refs('home:docs/d.md')]
        self.assertNotIn(('commit', '960c8c4b'), kinds)
        self.assertNotIn(('path', '.tsv'), kinds)

                         ['Q1', 'home:docs/lonely.md'])

input.content:
# linkcheck

Resolves the references between Markdown documents across Praxis, anthropic-pbc
and Dark, offline and deterministically. Built after Sloane, 2026-11-05:
"Linked identity, resolve it in code." That day four documents were linked by
hand and a contradiction between two of them was found by reading. This tool
finds it from the bytes.

    python3 linkcheck/linkcheck.py check --case linkcheck/cases/identity-ring.tsv
    python3 linkcheck/linkcheck.py check --report praxis:OPENQUESTIONS.md
    python3 -m unittest linkcheck/test_linkcheck.py

Stdlib Python, PEP 723 (`uv run linkcheck/linkcheck.py ...` also works). No
network. Git is used read-only (`rev-parse`, `cat-file -e`, `show`). It never
checks out, so it can read Dark's `claude/identity-ring` branch without
touching that worktree.

## What it checks

**1. References resolve.** Each reference is reported with file and line.

| Reference | Found as | Resolved by |
|---|---|---|
| path | a code span or Markdown link with a known extension, or ending in `/` | the file exists at the ref (`git cat-file -e`), or on disk for a working-tree document |
| path in another repo | `` `repo:path` ``; the repo's name just before the span (`` Dark `docs/x.md` ``); or a first segment naming a repo (`praxis/OPENQUESTIONS.md`) when the path is absent from the document's own repo | as above, in that repo, at its `HEAD` |
| path at a branch | `` branch `name` `` after the path in the same paragraph or list item | at `name`, falling back to `origin/name` |
| open question | `Q30`, against headings `### Q30 ·` in `--questions` (default `praxis:OPENQUESTIONS.md`) | the heading exists. Outside Praxis, only on a line that says "question", "Praxis" or "OPENQUESTIONS", so a quarter like Q3 is not misread |
| commit | 7 to 40 lower-case hex with a letter and a digit, not followed by `…` (a truncated digest) | the commit exists in the repo of the nearest earlier path in the paragraph, else the document's repo. A miss names any other repo that has it |
| trail | `trail 10`, `trail #10`, `trail ... #10` | a snapshot TSV given with `--trails` (`number<TAB>title`). Trails live on the Entire server, so without a snapshot they are UNCHECKED |

A path in prose is tried from the repository root, then from the document's
directory and each directory above it. A Markdown link is relative to its
document, as usual. Paths under `~` or `/`, and repositories not checked out,
are UNCHECKED, never counted as resolved.

**2. Reciprocity.** Under a `Related` heading (any level) or a `**Related:**`
list field, every listed Markdown document or open question must link back.
A back-link is a path that resolves to the source document, or, when the
source is a question section of `OPENQUESTIONS.md`, its Q-id. A one-way link
is reported as `ONE-WAY source -> target`.

**3. Assertion conflicts.** Explicit keys only; see the convention below.
Two assertions with the same key and different values are a CONFLICT, listed
with each source, its location and its date.

**Output** is sorted, carries no clock or host, and is byte-identical on
rerun against the same repository states. The exit code is 1 on any MISSING-DOC,
UNRESOLVED, ONE-WAY, ASSERTION problem or CONFLICT; `--report` prints the same
lines and exits 0. UNCHECKED never fails.

## The assertion convention

Inline, in a document this repository may edit: one HTML comment, on its own
line next to the prose it records.

    <!-- assert key=identity-ring.location value=collected date=2026-11-05 source="CIO direction 10" quote="with a specific name and location" by="llm:claude-opus-5-5 prompt=unrecorded" -->

`key`, `value`, `date` and `source` are required. `quote`, if present, must

touching that worktree.
